sw-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone: Case Management for a Multi-Problem Household and a Program Proposal
explain: The final lesson is a task not of hitting a fixed right answer but of weaving together what has been learned into a single product. The task has two parts. First, read a fictional multi-problem household case and draw up a case management plan. Next, write a proposal for a community program for households facing the same difficulty. All institutions and figures are fictional, and this is not advice on using any real program or on intervention.

The case is as follows. The Baram household of Byeollae City, Galaxia, consists of a 52-year-old father, a 49-year-old mother, and a 14-year-old child. The father lost his job three months ago, and the mother has cut back her work to care for parents with limited mobility. The child's absences from school have increased. Rent is overdue, and the household hesitates greatly to ask for help. First note that there is also much that cannot be known in this case.

Write the case part using the process of Lessons 14 and 15. Distinguish facts from interpretations, organize needs, resources, and strengths, and draw the surrounding systems in an ecomap. Assume goals are set together with the person concerned, and if some needs have a different priority, write the reason. Classify the services to link as closer to social insurance, public assistance, or social services, and point out in which of the four dimensions of the policy analysis framework obstacles are likely. Also state how the principles of self-determination and confidentiality will be kept.

Write the proposal part using the framework of Lessons 17 and 18. The order of the framework is as follows.
1. Evidence for the problem and need: Write a community problem that can be generalized from the case, and give fictional figures as evidence.
2. Objectives: Write specific objectives so that the target group, period, and method of measurement are clear.
3. Logic model: Write inputs, activities, outputs, and outcomes separately.
4. Evaluation plan: Distinguish output indicators from outcome indicators, and set a comparison group or a baseline point.
5. Budget: Calculate amounts by item and the unit cost of an output.
6. Ethics and limits: Write consent, confidentiality, concern about stigma, and what is not known.

The budget calculation is simple. Hiring 2 staff at a monthly personnel cost of 3 million won for 12 months gives 2 × 300 × 12 = 72 million won (7,200 ten-thousand won), and adding operating costs of 6 million won gives a total of 78 million won. Dividing this total by the number of household visits gives the unit cost. What matters is not the calculation but whether you can explain how the numbers connect to the objectives and activities.

Evaluation is checking by yourself, with a checklist, how well this task was done. In the case part, check whether you distinguished facts from interpretations, saw strengths, and made a plan that respects the person's self-determination. In the proposal part, check whether the objectives are measurable, whether outputs and outcomes are distinguished, and whether the evaluation avoids overclaiming that the results are thanks to the program. Finally, develop the habit of stating the limits yourself, that is, which choice sacrifices other values.

examples.title: Example of Proposal Objectives and Outcome Indicators
body: Conditions (fictional): The general goal of the community program is "housing stability for households at risk of rent arrears."
Step 1 (specific objective): Of the households participating in the program, at least 60% will have fewer months of arrears within 12 months than at the start.

Step 2 (distinguishing indicators): The output indicator is the number of household visits, and the outcome indicator is the decrease in months of arrears. Interpretation: Even if the number of visits exceeds the target, if months of arrears do not decrease, there is no outcome.

examples.title: Distinguishing Facts from Interpretations in a Case
body: Conditions (fictional): Among the sentences in the case, "the father is lazy" is an interpretation, and "the father lost his job three months ago" is a fact.
Step 1: A fact is what is written in the case, and an interpretation is what the reader adds. Write the basis and the limits together with an interpretation.

Step 2: Also make a list of what is not known. For example, whether the household is already receiving some services is not in the case. Interpretation: Stating what is not known turns it into questions to check and becomes a safeguard against asserting conclusions.

checks.hint: Find the personnel cost first and add the operating costs.

checks.prompt: Write one objective of a program you would design, and in two or three sentences distinguish that objective's outcome indicator from its output indicator.
checks.hint: Recall the distinction between outputs and outcomes in Lesson 17.

checks.model: The goal is to help households at risk of arrears reduce their months of arrears within 12 months compared with the start. The outcome indicators are the decrease in months of arrears among participating households and the share of households that kept stable housing. The output indicators are the amount we provided, such as the number of household visits and the number of service linkages, and these alone cannot tell us about outcomes.
